media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A desert that sneaked into Colombia without asking anyone's permission.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this Colombian desert of reddish earth and dry canyons?
hints: It's in the south of the country, near the Magdalena River.
It's famous for its night sky: lots of people go there to stargaze.
It's in Huila, near Villavieja, and its name starts with “Ta”.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it's called a desert, the Tatacoa is actually a tropical dry forest.

media.credit: José A. Vaca B. · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José A. Vaca B.

questions.description: A party so good it won't fit in one night, so you have to repeat it with natilla and buñuelos.
questions.question: What day does the Novena de Aguinaldos start?
hints: It starts a few days after the Día de las Velitas.
It ends on December 24, Christmas Eve.
Count nine days back from Christmas Eve, counting Christmas Eve itself.
questions.fun_fact: The Novena de Aguinaldos was written by a friar about 240 years ago, and it's prayed mostly in Colombia and Ecuador.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A delicious fruit that, according to Colombian moms, you should never go around giving away.
questions.question: In Colombia, what are you being told when someone says “no dé papaya”?
questions.answer: Don't be careless or give others an advantage
wrong_answers: Share your food with everyone around you
Never tell lies to anyone at all
Hurry up and finish your homework
hints: It's advice for staying safe when you go out.
You'll hear it a lot if you walk around with your phone in your hand where everyone can see it.
It's the opposite of being distracted and too trusting, so someone else takes advantage.
questions.fun_fact: The saying has a second part, “a papaya puesta, papaya partida”: if someone gets careless, there's always somebody ready to take advantage.

media.credit: Maksym Kozlenko · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Maksym Kozlenko

questions.description: The month when Medellín smells better than any perfume counter at the mall.
questions.question: In which month is Medellín’s Feria de las Flores held?
hints: It’s in the second half of the year.
The Battle of Boyacá is remembered in the same month.
It comes right after July.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de las Flores isn’t only about flowers: it also has a parade of classic and antique cars that rolls through Medellín.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A town where moms live with their hearts in their mouths.
questions.question: Which Colombian town is famous as the capital of adventure sports?
hints: It's in Santander.
The Chicamocha Canyon is close by, and the Fonce River runs through the town.
Its name starts like a saint's name.
questions.fun_fact: In San Gil's El Gallineral park, the trees are covered in gray “barba de viejo” (old man's beard), a plant that hangs down like curtains.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A museum so valuable that even the security guards need security guards.
questions.question: Which museum in Bogotá keeps the famous Muisca Raft, a small figure of a chief and his companions on a raft?
hints: It was created by the Banco de la República and stands next to Parque Santander, in downtown Bogotá.
It has the world's largest collection of metal objects made by Indigenous peoples before the Spanish arrived.
Its name is that of the most famous shiny yellow metal.
questions.fun_fact: The Gold Museum holds more than 30,000 objects of gold and other metals made by Indigenous peoples of Colombia.

media.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Felipe Restrepo Acosta

questions.description: The one night a year nobody gets scolded for playing with fire on the sidewalk.
questions.question: On which night does Colombia celebrate Día de las Velitas, when families light candles and lanterns in windows and on sidewalks?
hints: It's one of the first celebrations of the Christmas season.
The next day is a public holiday in Colombia.
It's the eve of the Feast of the Immaculate Conception.
questions.fun_fact: In Quimbaya, Quindío, neighborhoods compete every year in a festival of candles and lanterns that fills the whole town with light.

media.credit: Holger Motzkau · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Holger Motzkau

questions.description: A hat with so many turns you get dizzy just looking at it.
questions.question: The sombrero vueltiao, a cultural symbol of Colombia, is woven from braids of a plant fiber. Which one?
hints: Zenú artisans weave it in Córdoba and Sucre, above all in Tuchín.
Its fibers are pale, and the black parts are dyed with mud and plant leaves.
Its Spanish name joins a long-stemmed plant with what a bow shoots.
questions.fun_fact: The more braid turns a sombrero vueltiao has (it can have 21, 23 or more), the finer and pricier it is.

media.credit: Fernan Acosta · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fernan Acosta

questions.description: Men who throw a whole garden on their backs like it's a school backpack.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what are these farmers called who parade through Medellín carrying huge flower displays on their backs?
hints: They parade every August at the Feria de las Flores.
They come from Santa Elena, a rural district in the mountains above Medellín.
Their name comes from the wooden frame they carry, which looks like a chair.
questions.fun_fact: The Desfile de Silleteros has been held since 1957, and some silletas are so big they weigh more than 60 kg (130 lb).

media.credit: SajoR · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SajoR

questions.description: This person gives you hugs on every birthday, and nothing else.
questions.question: In Colombia, what do people call a very stingy person, someone who won't even lend you a pencil?
hints: The word is also the name of something we all have on our body.
People say this person's arm is so stiff it won't bend to reach for the money in their pocket.
It's the part of the arm between the hand and the shoulder, right where it bends.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico a stingy person is called the same thing, and to say it without words, people tap that part of their arm.

media.credit: stevepb · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: stevepb

questions.description: Three weeks of pedaling around France, and at the end they give you a yellow shirt: the deal of the century.
questions.question: Who was the first Colombian to win the Tour de France?
hints: He won it in 2019 and was one of the youngest champions ever.
He was born in Bogotá and grew up in Zipaquirá, the town with the Salt Cathedral.
His first name starts with E and his last name rhymes with “canal”.
questions.fun_fact: Egan Bernal won the Tour de France at just 22, and before racing on the road he was a mountain biker.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.description: A climb so long you start in the lowland heat and finish begging for a ruana.
questions.question: Which Colombian climb, about 80 km (50 miles) long, is considered by many cyclists the longest paved climb in the world?
hints: It climbs from Tolima toward the department of Caldas.
It starts in Mariquita, in the hot lowlands, and reaches more than 3,600 m (11,800 ft).
Its name in Spanish means what the alphabet is made of.
questions.fun_fact: Riding up Alto de Letras, you go from the heat of the lowlands to the cold of the páramo: several climates in a single day of pedaling!

media.credit: Alejandro  Bayer Tamayo from Armenia, Colombia · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alejandro  Bayer Tamayo from Armenia, Colombia

questions.description: A sport named after a town, as if soccer were called “Fusagasugá”.
questions.question: Tejo used to be called “turmequé” too, after the name of a town. Which department is that town in?
hints: It's a department of cold mountains, on the high plateau where the Muisca lived.
Its capital is Tunja.
In 1819 it was the site of the battle that sealed Colombia's independence.
questions.fun_fact: The Muisca played something like tejo centuries ago, and the story goes that they threw discs of stone or gold.

media.credit: Mussi Katz · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mussi Katz

questions.description: A piece of Colombia highlighted, like when you underline the important part before a test.
questions.question: Look at the map: which department of Colombia is highlighted?
hints: It's in the far south of Colombia.
A little tip of it reaches a giant river, on the border with Brazil and Peru.
Its capital is Leticia.
questions.fun_fact: Amazonas is Colombia's largest department, but one of the least populated.

media.credit: Elkin Fricke · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Elkin Fricke

questions.description: A department so indecisive it couldn't pick just one ocean.
questions.question: What is the only department of Colombia with a coast on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean?
hints: It's in the west of the country, and almost all of it is rainforest.
It's one of the rainiest places on the planet.
It's the only department that borders Panama.
questions.fun_fact: It rains so much in Chocó that it ranks among the rainiest places in the whole world.

media.credit: leonardo cadavid perdomo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: leonardo cadavid perdomo

questions.description: They ride up mountains faster than your dad climbs the stairs after lunch.
questions.question: What nickname have Colombian cyclists, famous for how well they climb mountains, had for decades?
hints: The nickname is the name of an animal.
It's an animal much smaller than a bicycle.
It's an insect with a hard shell; some roll little balls of dung.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Herrera, one of the most famous escarabajos, won the Alpe d'Huez stage in 1984 and became the first Colombian to win a stage of the Tour de France.

media.credit: Inyang Effiong · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Inyang Effiong

questions.description: An aiming game so corner-store that it practically comes with a soda.
questions.question: What is the corner-store game where you toss metal disks into the holes of a wooden table?
hints: It's played a lot in small-town stores and courts, often right next to tejo.
The hole worth the most points is in the mouth of a little metal figure.
The figure is a green animal that hops and goes “ribbit.”
questions.fun_fact: In Peru it's played almost the same way, but there they call it “el sapo” (the toad).

media.credit: Chicken4War · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chicken4War

questions.description: Colombia's national sport: throwing a metal disc into a pit of clay and celebrating like it's a goal.
questions.question: In tejo, little “mechas” are placed around the bocín. What are the mechas made of?
hints: They sit on the edge of the bocín, in the clay pit.
When the tejo hits one, the whole place knows it from the noise.
They hold the same stuff as the totes and voladores of December.
questions.fun_fact: Mechas are small triangles, and setting one off scores more points than just landing near the bocín.

media.credit: Matt Zimmerman · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matt Zimmerman

questions.description: In Cali, people dance salsa so fast that their shoes ask for a vacation.
questions.question: In which month is the Feria de Cali held, with its famous parade of salsa dancers?
hints: It's a time of year when many Colombians are on vacation.
In this month, many homes fill up with lights and nativity scenes.
It starts on the 25th and ends before the year is over.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de Cali began in 1957 and today opens with the Salsódromo, a parade with hundreds of salsa dancers.

media.credit: Jyon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jyon

questions.description: A traveler of the plains who never goes empty-handed, though you'd better hope he doesn't show you what he's carrying.
questions.question: Which ghost of the Llanos legends is very tall and skinny, roams the plains at night, and carries his own father's bones in a sack?
hints: It's a legend from the Llanos Orientales, which Colombia shares with Venezuela.
They say that if you hear him close by, he's actually far away.
His name comes from a sound he makes with his lips.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says El Silbón whistles the notes do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, which is why hearing someone whistle the scale on the plains at night is so frightening.

media.credit: Basotxerri · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Basotxerri

questions.description: Jumping on the bed doesn't count as Olympic training, no matter how hard you try.
questions.question: In which track and field event did Caterine Ibargüen win gold at the Rio 2016 Olympics?
hints: It's a jumping event where you land in a sand pit.
Before landing in the sand, you make several bounds in a row: hop, step and jump.
The event's name tells you how many jumps you make: three.
questions.fun_fact: Four years earlier, at London 2012, Caterine had already won silver in the same event.

media.credit: Donatas Dabravolskas · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Donatas Dabravolskas

questions.description: Before her, Colombia kept its gold medals in the same place as the unicorns.
questions.question: Who was the first Colombian woman to win an Olympic gold medal?
hints: She did it at the Sydney Olympics in 2000.
Her sport is all about lifting very, very heavy bars.
She's a weightlifter from Valle del Cauca who later became a member of Congress.
questions.fun_fact: That gold at Sydney 2000 was also Colombia's first Olympic gold ever, counting both men and women.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.description: A river that dives headfirst from over 100 meters up and doesn't even scream.
questions.question: Which river plunges over the famous Tequendama Falls, in Cundinamarca?
hints: It starts in a páramo in Cundinamarca, in the town of Villapinzón.
Before reaching the falls, it flows past the country's biggest city.
It has the same name as Colombia's capital.
questions.fun_fact: Tequendama Falls is about 157 m (515 ft) high, and the old mansion next to it is now a museum.

media.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Felipe Restrepo Acosta

questions.description: A year when the whole country shouted so loud that the neighbors in Panama asked for some quiet.
questions.question: In which year did Colombia's senior national team win its first Copa América, playing at home?
hints: That year, Colombia hosted the tournament.
The final was in Bogotá against Mexico, and Colombia won 1–0.
It was the first year of the 21st century.
questions.fun_fact: In that Copa América, Colombia won all six of its matches without letting in a single goal.

media.credit: Futbolero · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Futbolero

questions.description: Thousands of fans shouting at once: here even your eardrums break a sweat.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this stadium, the usual home of Colombia's national team in World Cup qualifiers?
hints: Visiting teams don't like playing there because of the heat and humidity.
It's on the Caribbean coast, near where the Magdalena River meets the sea.
It's in Barranquilla and is named after a Barranquilla-born soccer player, Roberto Meléndez.
questions.fun_fact: Many visiting teams complain about Barranquilla's heat and humidity, which is why the national team prefers to play its most important games there.

media.credit: Mkstillo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mkstillo

questions.description: No barber ever dared to touch this hairdo.
questions.question: Which player is this? A Colombian midfielder with a huge curly blond mane, famous for his magical passes and for barely running.
hints: He was the national team's great idol in the 1990s.
He wore the number 10 shirt and played at the 1990, 1994 and 1998 World Cups.
He is from Santa Marta, and everyone knows him as “el Pibe.”
questions.fun_fact: In Santa Marta, his hometown, there is a giant bronze statue of el Pibe, mane and all.

media.credit: StellaInfante · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: StellaInfante

questions.description: A pig that showed up to the party full of itself. Literally.
questions.question: Lechona, the famous stuffed pig, is a typical dish of which Colombian department?
hints: It's a department in the center of the country, with no coastline.
The Magdalena River crosses its hot, flat lowlands, and its mountains have a snow-capped volcano.
Its capital is Ibagué, the “Musical Capital of Colombia.”
questions.fun_fact: A big lechona can feed more than 50 people, which is why it rules at family parties.

media.credit: Karl Gruber · CC BY-SA 3.0 at · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Karl Gruber

questions.description: Even Colombia's biggest river needs a friend to help carry the water.
questions.question: What is the largest tributary of the Magdalena River, the one that gives it the most water?
hints: It rises in the Colombian Massif, very close to where the Magdalena itself begins.
It runs from south to north through the valley where Cali lies.
It has the same name as the department whose capital is Popayán.
questions.fun_fact: The Cauca and the Magdalena run almost parallel for more than 1,000 km (620 miles), separated by the Cordillera Central, and only meet near Mompox.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A bus that went out partying and never got serious again.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this colorful painted wooden vehicle, typical of Colombian towns, called?
hints: It has ladders on the outside to climb up to the roof, where bags and sacks are loaded.
In many cities you can rent one for parties, with music and people dancing inside.
Its name is also the Spanish word for a goat.
questions.fun_fact: In small towns, the chiva carries all sorts of things on its roof: sacks of coffee, bunches of plantains, and sometimes even chickens.

media.credit: https://www.flickr.com/people/pat_ossa/ · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: https://www.flickr.com/people/pat_ossa/

questions.description: The dessert that shakes with fear every December because it knows it's about to be eaten.
questions.question: What is Colombian Christmas natilla made from?
hints: It's almost always eaten next to buñuelos.
It's cooked in a pot and stirred nonstop until it gets thick.
It has a dark brown sugarcane sweet and a white powder that comes from corn.
questions.fun_fact: In many homes, natilla is stirred for a long time in a big paila, and you can't stop stirring or it sticks to the pan.

media.credit: Akire gatuna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Akire gatuna

questions.description: In this region “ajá” works as a greeting, a question, a complaint and a yes, all at once.
questions.question: In Colombia, what are people called who talk with “ajá”, “eche” and “¡qué nota!”?
hints: They're named after the region of Colombia they come from.
They live near the Caribbean Sea, where it's hot all year.
The word comes from “costa”.
questions.fun_fact: Costeños often “swallow” the s at the end of words, so “los cocos” can sound like “lo' coco'”.

media.credit: Camilo1982 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Camilo1982

questions.description: A founding father who, instead of a statue, got thousands of students with ID cards.
questions.question: I'm a university in Bogotá named after the first president of the State of Cundinamarca, in 1811. Which one am I?
hints: My name is a person's full name.
That founding father was the son of the Marquis of San Jorge.
Many people just call me “la Tadeo”.
questions.fun_fact: The university bearing his name was founded in Bogotá in 1954, almost 140 years after his presidency.

media.credit: Jimmy Gómez N · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jimmy Gómez N

questions.description: A city tucked into a giant cooking pot, but a pretty one, with mountains for a lid.
questions.question: “The Sabana is to Bogotá as the Valle de Aburrá is to…”. Which city completes the sentence?
hints: It's a city in Antioquia.
A river with the same name as the city runs along the bottom of that valley.
It's the city of the Metrocable and the Feria de las Flores.
questions.fun_fact: The Valle de Aburrá isn't home to just one city: ten municipalities share it, joined in one metropolitan area.

media.credit: Hernán Enrique Carvajal Cortés from Paris, France · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hernán Enrique Carvajal Cortés from Paris, France

questions.description: A flower named after a Swedish baron and an Andean empire, both at once.
questions.question: It's called the “lily of the Incas,” and its petals have little stripes that look hand-painted. What is this flower called in Colombia?
hints: It's native to South America and grown in huge numbers on the Sabana de Bogotá and in Antioquia.
It's very common in the bouquets sold in supermarkets and flower shops.
Its name sounds a bit like “astro,” as in the stars.
questions.fun_fact: Cut astromelias can last about two weeks in a vase, which is why florists love them.

media.credit: Mariaalejandragallego · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mariaalejandragallego

questions.description: The reason every dog in the neighborhood hides under the bed in December.
questions.question: In Colombia, what one word covers voladores, totes and luces de bengala?
hints: It makes a lot of noise and fills the sky with lights.
Kids should never handle it, because it can burn.
It's also the Spanish word for gunpowder.
questions.fun_fact: Gunpowder was invented in China more than a thousand years ago.

media.credit: Staticshakedown · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Staticshakedown

questions.description: One of these names snuck into the fruit bowl, but it really came in a glass.
questions.question: You're reading the menu at a juice stand on Colombia's coast. Which of these names is NOT a fruit?
hints: Three grow on a tree or plant; the other comes out of the blender.
The odd one out is served cold and has milk in it.
It's made by blending guanábana (soursop) with milk and sugar.
questions.fun_fact: Guanábana champola is typical of Colombia's Caribbean coast, and Cuba has a drink with the same name.

media.credit: Dr. Thomas Liptak · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dr. Thomas Liptak

questions.description: Some goals get celebrated once, and some your dad keeps celebrating at every family lunch.
questions.question: In what year did James score his famous chest-and-volley goal against Uruguay that sent Colombia to the World Cup quarterfinals?
hints: It was at a World Cup where James finished as the top scorer.
That World Cup was played in South America, in Colombia's biggest neighbor.
It was the same World Cup where Germany beat Brazil 7–1.
questions.fun_fact: That goal won FIFA's Puskás Award for the best goal of 2014.

media.credit: Agência Brasil · CC BY 3.0 br · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Agência Brasil

questions.description: At that age, some people are just learning to brew a tinto, and others are already scoring at World Cups.
questions.question: How old was Linda Caicedo when she scored a stunning goal against Germany at the 2023 Women's World Cup?
hints: She was one of the youngest players on the team.
The year before, she also played in both the U-17 and U-20 World Cups.
She had only just reached voting age in Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia beat Germany 2–1 in that match, with a header by Manuela Vanegas in the final seconds.

media.credit: Diplomatic Security Service from Washington, D.C., United States of America · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diplomatic Security Service from Washington, D.C., United States of America

questions.description: A family photo where somebody clearly wandered into the wrong picture.
questions.question: Which of these people is not from Colombia's Andean region?
hints: The odd one out lives near the sea, not in the mountains.
Their department is one of the rainiest places in the world.
Its capital is Quibdó.
questions.fun_fact: Chocó is one of the rainiest places on Earth: in some areas it rains almost every day of the year.

media.credit: Servicio Geológico Colombiano · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Servicio Geológico Colombiano

questions.description: It looks like a rough brown rock on the outside, but it's one of the sweetest things at the market.
questions.question: What is the flesh of the zapote like?
questions.answer: Orange and fibrous, with large seeds
wrong_answers: White and creamy, with black seeds
Yellow and jelly-like, with small seeds
Red and watery, with small black seeds
hints: It grows on a tree in hot climates.
On the outside it has a rough, greenish-brown skin.
Its flesh is about the color of a tangerine.
questions.fun_fact: Zapote flesh is so fibrous that eating it leaves little threads stuck between your teeth.

media.credit: Erasmus Kamugisha · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Erasmus Kamugisha

questions.description: A word that works just as well for a broken heart as for Grandma's kitchen.
questions.question: Taken literally, what is a «tusa»?
questions.answer: The empty core of an ear of corn
wrong_answers: The peel of a green plantain
The large seed of an avocado
The hard stone of a mango
hints: Karol G and Nicki Minaj used it in a song about heartbreak, but here we mean the literal thing.
You throw it away after eating, and it comes from a plant whose food grows wrapped in leaves.
It's what's left in your hand when you finish a grilled ear from a street cart in the park.
questions.fun_fact: That's why Colombians say someone «está con la tusa»: they're left empty, like the cob after all the kernels have been eaten.

media.credit: PinkBeachPlanet · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PinkBeachPlanet

questions.description: A classic danced so often in December that it should have its own ID card and a pension by now.
questions.question: Complete: Grupo Niche is to “Cali pachanguero” as Fruko y sus Tesos is to…
hints: The song was recorded by the Discos Fuentes label from Medellín.
It was sung by Wilson “Saoko” Manyoma, in a mournful voice.
It tells the story of someone locked up in a jail.
questions.fun_fact: The great Joe Arroyo began his career singing with Fruko y sus Tesos before starting his own orchestra.

media.credit: Franz van Duns · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Franz van Duns

questions.description: A veteran stadium that has seen more goals and more queens than any other in the neighborhood.
questions.question: In which city, near where the Magdalena River reaches the sea, is the Estadio Romelio Martínez?
hints: Every year the queen of a very famous festival is crowned there.
It was home to the team nicknamed “el Tiburón” (the Shark) until 1986.
It's the city of the Batalla de Flores and the Marimonda.
questions.fun_fact: Junior left the Romelio Martínez when the Estadio Metropolitano, one of Colombia's biggest stadiums, opened.

media.credit: Fragglerock52 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fragglerock52

questions.description: The moment of the party when even Grandpa puts on a colorful hat.
questions.question: At a Colombian quinceañera, costumed characters suddenly burst in with whistles, foam, lights and giant hats. What has just started?
hints: It usually comes late at night, when the party is already heating up.
There are stilts, masks, glow necklaces and music at full blast.
Its name says that for a while everyone goes a little crazy.
questions.fun_fact: The hora loca is so popular at Colombian parties that some companies do nothing but run it.

media.credit: Alex Sims · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alex Sims

questions.description: A fruit with two moms and zero family drama.
questions.question: A mule is to a mare and a donkey as the atemoya is to the cherimoya and… which other fruit?
hints: The two fruits in the mix are cousins: same family, white flesh and black seeds.
The other mom is small and green, with skin covered in little scales.
Elsewhere it's called saramuyo or sugar apple; in Colombia its name has just four letters and sounds like “anona”.
questions.fun_fact: The atemoya was first bred on purpose in Florida in the early 1900s (around 1907), and its name blends “ate” (another name for the anón) with “cherimoya”.

media.credit: Hannes Grobe 21:22, 5 November 2006 (UTC) · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hannes Grobe 21:22, 5 November 2006 (UTC)

questions.description: A perfect vacation plan until someone asks: “Wait, did you bring your passport?”
questions.question: Which of these Spanish forts, built against pirates, is NOT on Colombia's Caribbean coast?
questions.answer: Castillo de San Lorenzo del Chagres

questions.fun_fact: Many Indigenous peoples of the Colombian Amazon believed that shamans could turn into jaguars.

questions.fun_fact: This cleansing ritual is practiced in many Latin American countries, from Mexico to Colombia.

questions.description: The only itch everyone wants to have.
questions.question: Finish the Colombian superstition: “If the palm of your hand itches…”
hints: It's about something you receive with your hand.

You keep it in your wallet.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions the hand matters: one hand means money coming in, the other means money going out.

media.author: Eyefive45

hints: The “cuajo” is supposed to be a part of the belly.

questions.fun_fact: To “fix” a descuajado baby, tradition takes it to a sobandera, who rubs it and sometimes turns it upside down.

I'm half girl.

media.author: SanLuis2522

hints: People use me to talk about a part of the face.

It starts with B and has two syllables.

questions.description: Words that arrived without a passport but with plenty of style.

The name comes from Gaul, the old name of that land.

It's a short word that comes from “paisano.”
questions.fun_fact: The word “paisa” comes from “paisano,” meaning someone from the same land.

Its capital is Pasto.

media.author: Elkin Fricke

questions.description: A relative you won't find on the family tree, but you'll find at every party.
questions.question: He's your child's godfather, your dad calls his best friend this, and vallenato songs say it all the time. What's the word?
hints: It starts at a baptism.

Think of a “father” shared with someone else.
questions.fun_fact: “Compadre” comes from the Latin “compater”, meaning “father together with another”.

media.author: Jdvillalobos

hints: The nickname came from the empire that ruled their lands.

hints: He was a very popular political leader of the mid-20th century.

His face is on the 1,000-peso bill.
questions.fun_fact: The Salón Nacional de Artistas is Colombia's oldest art exhibition, and it is still held today.

media.author: Guangywatchwii

questions.description: A painting so famous it gave its name to a whole town… or was it the other way around?

questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the painting was miraculously “renewed” on December 26, 1586, getting back the colors it had lost.

hints: It comes from a colonial city south of Colombia.

Today that city is the capital of Ecuador.
questions.fun_fact: Caspicara, one of the great sculptors of that school, was an Indigenous man whose name in Quechua is said to mean “wooden face”.

questions.description: Basements with spiral staircases, and not a single piece of old junk stored in them.

It starts with the same four letters as “hypothermia”.

questions.fun_fact: “Musa paradisiaca” is the scientific name that Linnaeus gave to the plantain.

My last name is the same as that of a Venezuelan general who fought alongside Bolívar.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá's School of Fine Arts is now part of the National University of Colombia.

You share secrets and jokes with them that nobody else gets.
They play with you at recess.
questions.fun_fact: This saying appears in Don Quixote, spoken by Sancho Panza: “Dime con quién andas, decirte he quién eres.”

questions.description: A wise man who measured mountains with a pot, just like any grandma in the kitchen.
questions.question: I was born in Popayán, I measured the height of mountains with boiling water, and Bogotá's Universidad Distrital is named after me. Who am I?
hints: People called me “el Sabio” (the Wise One).
I took part in the Botanical Expedition and was a hero of Independence.
A department in the Coffee Region also carries my last name.
questions.fun_fact: Caldas found that the higher up you are, the lower the temperature at which water boils, and he used this to work out how high a place was.

questions.description: Before news popped up on your phone, it arrived on paper, at the speed of patience.

hints: It was founded by a librarian who had come from Cuba.
It came out around the time of the French Revolution.
It was at the end of the 18th century.
questions.fun_fact: It came out weekly and ran for about six years, until 1797.

media.credit: Roman Savulyak · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Roman Savulyak

questions.description: A Bogotá idea that took its inspiration from Australia without needing a passport.
questions.question: In the kangaroo mother care method, created in Bogotá: the pouch is to a baby kangaroo as what is to a premature baby?

What matters is warmth and skin-to-skin contact.
The baby stays pressed against its mom, day and night.
questions.fun_fact: Pediatrician Edgar Rey Sanabria created it in 1978 at the Instituto Materno Infantil in Bogotá, and today it is used in hospitals around the world.

media.author: SuperJew

questions.description: A little cube that left Bogotá and didn't stop until it reached space.
questions.question: Libertad 1, a satellite just 10 cm (4 in) across built in Bogotá, was the first Colombian one in orbit. In which decade was it launched?
hints: Cell phones with cameras already existed.
It was in the 21st century.
It was launched in 2007.
questions.fun_fact: Libertad 1 was built by students at Universidad Sergio Arboleda and launched from Kazakhstan.

media.author: Svobodat

questions.description: A virus named after a forest, with a mosquito's bad reputation.
questions.question: In what year did the Zika epidemic that put all of Colombia on alert reach the country?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
It was shortly before the Rio de Janeiro Olympic Games.
It was a few years before the COVID-19 pandemic.
questions.fun_fact: Zika is named after the Zika Forest in Uganda, where the virus was discovered in 1947.

hints: It is spread by a mosquito.
It is caused by a parasite called Plasmodium.
Its name comes from old Italian words for “bad air”.
questions.fun_fact: Patarroyo donated the patent for his SPf66 vaccine to the World Health Organization.

questions.question: This map from 1500 is the oldest surviving one to show the Americas. Which navigator made it and later explored Colombia's coast?
hints: He sailed with Christopher Columbus on his first voyages.
He owned the ship Santa María.
His last name contains the Spanish word for “thing.”
questions.fun_fact: The original map is kept at the Museo Naval in Madrid and is drawn on animal skin.

media.author: Juan de la Cosa

questions.description: The country's biggest university has a few years behind it, though you can't spot the gray hairs.
questions.question: In which century was the Universidad Nacional de Colombia founded?
hints: It was founded when Colombia was already independent.
It was during the United States of Colombia.
It was in 1867.
questions.fun_fact: Its Bogotá campus is nicknamed “la Ciudad Blanca” (the White City) for the color of its buildings.

media.author: Quervograf

questions.question: In Colombia, people from Antioquia are “antioqueños”. What are people from Caldas called?
hints: It's the word for people from Manizales and the area around it.
It's also used for the coffee and the landscapes of that department.
It ends the same way as “costarricense” (Costa Rican).
questions.fun_fact: The department of Caldas is named after the scholar Francisco José de Caldas.

media.author: XalD

questions.description: A candy with a hidden surprise, like a chocolate egg but on a stick.
questions.question: It's round, it has a stick, and when you finish the candy on the outside you find gum inside. What is it?
hints: It's a very famous Colombian candy sold in every neighborhood store.
It's made by Colombina.
It's a lollipop.
questions.fun_fact: Bon Bon Bum hit the market in 1970 and today is sold in dozens of countries.

media.author: Jim Larrison from Glen Ellyn, IL, USA

hints: I'm an aerospace engineer.
I work at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
My last name is also the name of a city in Peru.
questions.fun_fact: It was NASA's first Spanish-language broadcast of a landing on another planet, in February 2021.

questions.description: Grandma's favorite wrapping, long before aluminum foil came along.

hints: The food cooks inside it.
It gets tied up with string before it goes in to boil.
Think of a Sunday breakfast in Tolima, with hot chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: You don't eat the plantain leaf, but it gives tamales a special aroma while they cook.

media.author: BayoCine

questions.description: It got squashed, fried all over again, and came out happier than ever.
questions.question: These are patacones, like the ones eaten all over Colombia. What are they made of?
hints: It's a fruit, but it isn't eaten raw.
It's related to the banana.
It isn't ripe yet.
questions.fun_fact: To make patacones, the plantain is fried twice: first in chunks, then again after it's flattened.

media.author: Jdvillalobos

questions.question: Pan tajado comes in a bag, already cut into slices and ready for a sandwich. What flour is it almost always made from?

It comes from a cereal that grows in golden ears.
Almost all pan francés is made with this same flour.
questions.fun_fact: The first machine for slicing bread went on sale in the United States in 1928.

questions.description: It walks the whole beach under the midday sun and still never stops smiling.

hints: In the coastal heat, people are very grateful for it.
It's the vendor's most important tool when the sun is at its strongest.
Whatever they pull out of it is nice and icy.
questions.fun_fact: Styrofoam is almost all air, which is why it's so light and keeps heat out so well.

media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A saying for people who go back for seconds, and then for seconds of their seconds.

hints: It's not something you eat.
The saying is about how something works when it's brand new, before it wears out.
When it's new, it “eats” through wood or metal very fast.
questions.fun_fact: A new file has very sharp teeth, so it wears everything down as if it had an endless appetite.

hints: It's not the same dough as an arepa.
It's boiled and then mashed while still hot to make the dough.
The same root is eaten boiled in sancocho.
questions.fun_fact: The carimañola is a faithful partner of the coastal breakfast, alongside the arepa de huevo and coffee.

media.author: Grueslayer

questions.description: The only plantain that gets better once it gets spots.

hints: They come with a bandeja paisa.
They turn golden and a little sticky.
Their name comes from the Spanish verb “tajar”, which means to cut.
questions.fun_fact: The blacker the ripe plantain's peel, the sweeter the tajadas turn out.

media.author: Vis M

questions.question: Colombian bakeries sell a soft yellow cake in little squares that crumbles easily. It's made with cornstarch, eggs and sugar. What is it called?
hints: You can find it in almost any neighborhood bakery.
It's usually sold in portions wrapped in paper or plastic.
Its name sounds like “manteca”.
questions.fun_fact: Mantecada is usually eaten with tinto or hot chocolate at onces, the afternoon snack.

media.author: Andre.o.mob

hints: It's white.
It's made from milk.
It gets stretchy and melted when you scoop it out with your spoon.
questions.fun_fact: Aguapanela is also drunk cold with lime, like a panela lemonade!

It has lots of little kernels in rows.
The dried kernels of this plant are used to make crispetas (popcorn).
questions.fun_fact: The word “chócolo” comes from Quechua, like “choclo,” which is what tender corn is called in Peru and other Andean countries.

media.author: William Neuheisel from DC, US

It's cooked before being left to ferment.
It's the same white grain that comes with almost every Colombian lunch.

media.author: Tim Johnson from Savannah, GA, USA

questions.question: The first verse of Colombia's anthem says: “The horrible night has ended! Sublime liberty pours out the auroras of its invincible light.” What time of day does it describe?
hints: Look at who wins the fight: darkness or light.
“Has ended” tells you the night has just finished.
An “aurora” here is the glow in the sky before the sun comes up.
questions.fun_fact: The “horrible night” in the anthem stands for the time of Spanish rule before independence.

media.author: Alexander Gerst

questions.description: Two words every teacher would love to see written on the classroom board.
questions.question: Which Colombian national symbol has the motto “Libertad y Orden” written on it?
hints: You can see it on official documents and government buildings.
A condor holds a ribbon with the motto on it.
It has three sections and some flags on each side.
questions.fun_fact: The coat of arms shows the Isthmus of Panama because when it was designed in 1834, Panama was part of Colombia.

media.author: Andrea Gaetano

questions.description: A problem that leaves the rivers of the Pacific coast looking like they never want to get out of bed.
questions.question: It poisons rivers with mercury, leaves dredge holes in Chocó and the Amazon, and led to the Atrato River being declared a subject of rights. What is it?
hints: Park rangers and the security forces go after it.
It's looking for something at the bottom of rivers.
Its main goal is to get gold.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, Colombia's Constitutional Court declared the Atrato River a subject of rights, something almost no river in the world had.

media.author: CHOColombia

questions.description: Five rings and not a single wedding.
questions.question: Which of these colors does NOT appear in the Olympic rings?
hints: There are five rings of different colors on a white background.
All three colors of Colombia's flag are in the rings.
It's the color of grapes and eggplants.
questions.fun_fact: The ring colors, together with the white background, were chosen because they could be used to draw the flag of every country in the world at the time.

media.author: Edgar Jiménez

questions.description: A weight class where every gram counts and the scale is the most feared opponent.
questions.question: Ingrit Valencia won bronze at Rio 2016, the first Colombian female boxer with an Olympic medal, fighting in the lightest women's class of those Games. Which was it?
hints: At those Games, her class had a limit of 51 kg (112 lb).
It's named after an animal.
It's an insect that buzzes.
questions.fun_fact: At Rio 2016, women had only three boxing classes: 51, 60 and 75 kg (112, 132 and 165 lb).

media.author: U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Elliott Fabrizio

questions.description: In this sport, Colombia is like Brazil in soccer, just without the samba.
questions.question: Its champions race on tracks and streets, and Colombia has topped the country table at its World Championships again and again. What sport is it?
hints: Many Colombian children join clubs for it at a very young age.
The athletes wear helmets and special boots.
Under each boot is a row of small wheels.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has skating clubs in almost every city, and many champions started skating before the age of 6.

media.author: Jefferson Gutierrez Romero

questions.description: 21 kilometers (13 miles) that leave even the world's best distance runners begging for mercy.
questions.question: Elite runners from around the world say the Bogotá Half Marathon is one of the toughest on the planet. Why?
questions.answer: It's run at about 2,600 meters of altitude
wrong_answers: It goes up and down the eastern hills
It's always run in the rain
It has more than a hundred sharp turns
hints: The problem isn't the course, it's the air.
Runners who come from the coast feel it from the very first kilometer.
Bogotá is much closer to the clouds than to the sea.
questions.fun_fact: At Bogotá's height of about 2,600 m (8,500 ft), every breath brings in quite a bit less oxygen than at sea level, which is why many athletes train in the mountains.

questions.description: An orchid that poses for photos with the face of a cheeky monkey.
questions.question: Its flowers look like a monkey's face, it grows in cloud forests, and it is most diverse in Colombia and Ecuador. Which orchid genus is it?
hints: Its name comes from Latin.
Its sepals end in long, pointed tails.
It shares its name with the most famous vampire in the movies.
questions.fun_fact: “Dracula” means “little dragon” in Latin, after the long tails of its sepals, not after any vampire.

media.credit: Peter Angritt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Peter Angritt

questions.description: The prettiest and heaviest backpack ever carried in Antioquia.
questions.question: In Medellín's Desfile de Silleteros, how much can a giant silleta weigh?
hints: One single person carries it on their back.
It can be more than 2 meters (6.5 ft) wide.
It can weigh more than the person carrying it.
questions.fun_fact: The silleteros of Santa Elena learn the craft from their families, and some children parade with kid-size silletas from a very young age.

media.author: Mariaalejandragallego

questions.description: It flies more often than most business travelers, and always in refrigerated class.
questions.question: Colombia is one of the world's biggest exporters of this flower. Look at the close-up: which flower is it?
hints: Its petals have jagged edges.
It smells a little spicy.
Its Spanish name comes from the same word as the clove spice that goes into natilla.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish the carnation is called “clavel” after the “clavo de olor” (clove), because its scent is a reminder of it.

media.author: Takkk

questions.description: A whole garden walking through Medellín on somebody's back.
questions.question: In the Desfile de Silleteros, which category of silleta carries only bunches of flowers, with no figures or signs?
hints: It has no brands or ads.
It doesn't spell out messages or make pictures with flowers either.
It's put together the way the old silleteros of Santa Elena used to do it.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Feria existed, the farmers of Santa Elena used the silleta to carry flowers down to sell in Medellín.

questions.question: There's a tiple requinto, a requinto guitar and a requinto clarinet. What does “requinto” tell you about an instrument?
wrong_answers: It's an old version from colonial times
It only keeps the rhythm, never the melody
hints: The word comes from old Spanish, not from an Indigenous language.
In carranga, the requinto plays the picked melody above the tiple.
Think of a “child” instrument that sounds higher than its “parent.”
questions.fun_fact: In carranga, the tiple keeps the rhythm while the requinto decorates it with picked melodies.

media.author: Andrés Cabrera

questions.description: A question that tastes of sea breeze and arepa de huevo.
questions.question: Paisa is to “vos” as costeño is to…
hints: It's the word for talking to a friend, in a relaxed and familiar way.
It's the same one used in most songs.
It's the one Carlos Vives and Shakira use when they sing to someone.
questions.fun_fact: On the Caribbean coast “tú” is so common that many costeños use it even with people they've just met.

questions.question: In Pasto, in Boyacá and in Mexico, when someone calls your name, you answer “¿Mande?”. What does it mean?
hints: You say it to Mom, to the teacher and to your elders.
It comes from the Spanish verb “mandar,” to give orders.
It's like saying “I'm at your service.”
questions.fun_fact: “Mande” comes from “mandar”: it's like saying “give me your orders, I'm here to serve you.”

questions.description: Colombian words have more moods than a Monday holiday.
questions.question: Which of these Colombian expressions does NOT mean that something is good or fun?
hints: You'd say three of them at a great party.
You'd say the other one in a class that never ends.
In Colombia you say it when something is really boring or annoying.
questions.fun_fact: “Jartera” comes from “jartarse”, the popular form of “hartarse”: to be full of something or fed up with it.

media.credit: Andres Franco · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andres Franco

questions.description: Too big for the piñata, too small for a tinto.
questions.question: In Bogotá, this is the word for someone no longer a child but not yet an adult: in high school and always falling in love. What is it?
hints: This person is roughly between 12 and 17 years old.
Adults say it half fondly, half teasing, about kids starting to go to parties and have a boyfriend or girlfriend.
Its feminine form comes in a can.
questions.fun_fact: Rolos also say “chino” or “china” for a child or a young person.

media.author: Felipe Restrpo Acosta

questions.description: So many people live here that even the tinto has to wait in line.
questions.question: Most Colombians live in this region, three mountain ranges cross it, and Bogotá is there. Which region is it?
hints: It's the region of the mountains.
Medellín and Cali are there too.
It's named after the longest mountain range in South America.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the Andes split into three ranges: the Western, Central and Eastern Cordilleras.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: In Neiva in June, even the heat puts on a hat.
questions.question: At the Festival del Bambuco in Neiva, every candidate for queen must perform a sanjuanero. What is the sanjuanero?
hints: The candidates practice it for months.
It comes with band music and a handkerchief.
It's the signature tradition of Huila, and you need a partner for it.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival del Bambuco falls during the feasts of Saint John and Saint Peter, the most joyful celebrations of the year in Huila.

media.credit: CesarRincon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CesarRincon

questions.description: In Córdoba, when they say a band is about to play, they don't mean a rock band.
questions.question: At the Festival Nacional del Porro in San Pelayo, Córdoba, bandas sabaneras compete. Which instruments make up these bands?
questions.answer: Clarinets, trumpets, bass drum and cymbals
wrong_answers: Gaitas, maracas, tambor alegre and llamador
hints: They're the same bands that liven up corralejas and town fiestas.
Elsewhere they're called bandas papayeras.
They mix brass and woodwind instruments with band percussion.
questions.fun_fact: The bands of San Pelayo have played porro for generations, and the festival has been held every year since the late 1970s.

media.credit: Jaroldiazc19 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jaroldiazc19

questions.description: A song that has spent more than half a century sailing down the river without sinking.

The Festival Nacional de la Cumbia in El Banco is named after him.
questions.fun_fact: In “La piragua”, the boat travels between El Banco and Chimichagua, driven by twelve bogas (boatmen).

media.author: Timothy A. Gonsalves

My name puts together a salad vegetable and the place where I grow.
questions.fun_fact: Tomate de árbol is also called tamarillo, and it's a relative of the tomato and the potato.

media.credit: Horacio Cambeiro · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Horacio Cambeiro

questions.question: In Colombia, if people say someone “es como el arroz blanco” (is like white rice), what do they mean?
hints: The saying compares a person to the place rice has on the Colombian table.
It’s said jokingly and fondly about someone people know.
Just like rice at a Colombian meal, this person is never missing from anything.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia grows its own rice, mostly in the Llanos Orientales and in Tolima.

media.credit: Douglas Perkins · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Douglas Perkins

questions.question: Which freshwater fish, the most famous of the Magdalena River's subienda, is the star of a coastal sancocho?

Its mouth is very small.

Two juglares answer each other in verse to see who is better.

media.author: rothware

questions.description: A rural folk band that lost its bass player and built a new one from whatever grew in the hills.

questions.description: A word you pronounce with your hips.
