questions.fun_fact: In Chocó, the Atrato River is the main road for many towns: there, the motorboat is like a city bus.

media.credit: CHOColombia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CHOColombia

questions.description: The car said “this is as far as I go,” and nobody asked for its opinion.
questions.question: Look at the photo: in Colombia, when this happens to a car on the road, what word describes it?
hints: Something broke on the car and it won't start.
Time to call a tow truck or a mechanic.
The word comes from ships that get stuck on the sand.
questions.fun_fact: “Varar” comes from the world of ships: a “barco varado” is one that got stuck on the beach.

media.credit: ScoredBlock · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ScoredBlock

questions.description: Where the buses barely sleep and even the suitcases wait in line.
questions.question: You want to leave Bogotá's main bus terminal for the Caribbean coast without the crowds. Which time of year should you avoid?
hints: It's when lots of families go on vacation.
Most schools have finished the school year and the roads to the coast fill up.
It's the last month of the year.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá's Salitre bus terminal opened in 1984, and millions of travelers pass through it every year.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A tower that spends all night winking.
questions.question: In Santa Marta Bay, a traffic light is to cars as a lighthouse is to…
hints: It stands on the seashore.
Its light warns where there are rocks or where the port is.
They sail on the water.
questions.fun_fact: Facing Santa Marta Bay is El Morro, a rocky island with a lighthouse on top.

media.credit: Cesar Ivan Noreña Vega · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cesar Ivan Noreña Vega

questions.description: The first four-legged car arrived by ship, with no license plate.
questions.question: The Muisca, who lived on the Sabana de Bogotá, had never seen a horse. Who brought horses there?
hints: They came by sea about 500 years ago.
They arrived with the Conquest.
They spoke the same language people speak in Colombia today.
questions.fun_fact: Horses lived in the Americas millions of years ago but died out there, until the Spanish brought them back.

media.credit: Jusezam · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jusezam

questions.description: Small but loud, like the cousin who’s first to show up at the parranda.
questions.question: Vallenato blends three heritages. Which people gave it the caja, the small drum played by hand?
hints: This same heritage gave the Caribbean coast many other drums, like those of cumbia and mapalé.
This heritage reached the Caribbean coast through the port of Cartagena in colonial times.
Think of the heritage that brought drums to San Basilio de Palenque.
questions.fun_fact: The cajero plays sitting down, holding the caja between the knees.

media.credit: Wuselig · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wuselig

questions.description: A museum where the most valuable pieces have bellows and are ready to party.
questions.question: The Accordion Museum in Valledupar keeps instruments more than 100 years old. From which country did the first accordions reach Colombia's Caribbean coast?
hints: It's a European country.
They arrived on trading ships at ports like Riohacha in the late 19th century.
Hohner, the favorite brand of vallenato accordion players, comes from there.
questions.fun_fact: The museum was founded by accordion player Beto Murgas in his own home.

media.credit: --F3rn4nd0 06:17, 27 March 2007 (UTC) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: --F3rn4nd0 06:17, 27 March 2007 (UTC)

questions.description: Stockholm had never heard so much accordion on such a cold night.
questions.question: In 1982 García Márquez took vallenato musicians to Stockholm and accepted the Nobel wearing a white outfit. What is it called?
hints: It wasn't the tailcoat that protocol called for.
It's a suit with a high, closed collar, typical of the Llanos.
Its name repeats the same word twice.
questions.fun_fact: Gabo was one of the few winners that night who didn't accept the Nobel in a tailcoat.

media.credit: Jonas Bergsten · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jonas Bergsten

questions.description: A retired dinosaur who spends all day sunbathing in the park.
questions.question: I'm green, with a crest of spines on my back and a flap of skin under my chin, and I sunbathe in park trees in Cartagena and Santa Marta. Who am I?
hints: I am a reptile with a long tail.
I don't eat meat: I love leaves, flowers and fruit.
My name starts with the letter I.
questions.fun_fact: Iguanas are good swimmers and can hold their breath underwater for about half an hour.

media.credit: Adventourscolombia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adventourscolombia

questions.description: A tree that doesn't need high heels to stand out in every photo.
questions.question: You're in the Cocora Valley, standing before the wax palm, Colombia's national tree. How tall can it grow?
hints: It's considered the tallest palm in the world.
It's taller than a 15-story building.
It grows to more than 50 m (164 ft).
questions.fun_fact: The wax palm can live more than 100 years and is home to the yellow-eared parrot, which nearly disappeared.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A word that sounds like a silver mine and gets heard a lot at the repair shop.
questions.question: In Colombia, if fixing the car “costó un platal”, what happened to the owner?
questions.answer: They spent a ton of money
hints: It has nothing to do with the metal.
Nobody wants to hear it at the repair shop.
It's like saying it cost an arm and a leg.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, as in much of Latin America, “plata” (silver) means money, because centuries ago coins were made of that metal.

media.credit: SAgbley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SAgbley

questions.description: It's like a car, but it dressed up way too much for the party.
questions.question: You're at the Batalla de Flores of the Barranquilla Carnival and the biggest, most decorated float goes by. Who rides on top, waving?
hints: It's a person chosen especially for the carnival.
She wears a sparkly dress and often a crown.
Every year she is chosen and crowned before the parades.
questions.fun_fact: The Batalla de Flores was first held in 1903 and is the oldest parade of the Barranquilla Carnival.

media.credit: Ryan Hodnett · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ryan Hodnett

questions.description: In Pasto on January 6, nobody goes out without their secret weapon.
questions.question: Complete: at the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos, a “carioca” is a can of…
hints: It's used mostly on the Día de Blancos (Day of the Whites).
It comes out white and goes well with the talcum powder.
You press a button and it shoots out like shaving cream.
questions.fun_fact: The Carnaval de Negros y Blancos has been on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2009.

media.credit: Hanksol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hanksol

questions.description: An instrument with a duck’s beak and a bee’s head: the carnival has its own monsters.
questions.question: The Colombian gaita is a tube of cardón cactus with a beeswax head and a duck-feather quill; there are male and female gaitas. What kind of instrument is it?
hints: It has no strings and you don’t hit it.
Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto made it famous.
To make it sound, you need your lungs.
questions.fun_fact: Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto won a Latin Grammy in 2007.

media.credit: Jair Armando Beltrán Hernández · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jair Armando Beltrán Hernández

questions.description: Yesterday's newspaper gets a second life that's way more fun.
questions.question: Papier-mâché is made from newspaper and a paste of flour and water, then dried and painted. What is it used for at carnivals?
hints: When it dries, it's hard but light.
In Pasto, craftspeople spend months working with it in their workshops before the big parade on January 6.
You can cover your face with it or make a giant puppet.
questions.fun_fact: The giant floats of Pasto's Carnaval de Negros y Blancos are built mostly from papier-mâché, and some are taller than a house.

media.credit: Howard Lake from Colchester, UK · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Howard Lake from Colchester, UK

questions.description: Cantina music, wooden tables and not a single traffic jam in sight.
questions.question: At the Feria de las Flores, people set up fondas paisas. For whom were fondas first made, as roadside inns?
hints: They were travelers who crossed the mountains of Antioquia.
They carried loads from town to town for days.
They traveled with mules and wore a carriel and a poncho.
questions.fun_fact: The carriel, the arriero's leather bag, became one of the symbols of paisa culture.

media.credit: Mariaalejandragallego · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mariaalejandragallego

questions.description: The trophy that makes a dance group rehearse all year long.
questions.question: It's the top prize for the dance groups and comparsas of the Carnaval de Barranquilla, named after a dance with turbans and mirrors. What is it called?
hints: It's given to the best groups in the parades.
The dance it's named after uses very tall, decorated turbans.
Its name combines an African-rooted dance and a golden metal.
questions.fun_fact: The India Catalina, by contrast, is the award of the Cartagena International Film Festival.

media.credit: jonis e rodriguez r · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: jonis e rodriguez r

questions.description: A math problem dressed up as a Sunday at the ciclovía.
questions.question: In Colombia a bike is called a “cicla”. If a park has 4 ciclas and 2 tricycles, how many wheels are there in total?
hints: First count the wheels on the ciclas, then the ones on the tricycles.
Each cicla has 2 wheels and each tricycle has 3.
8 wheels from the ciclas plus 6 from the tricycles.
questions.fun_fact: “Cicla” is short for “bicicleta,” and Bogotá's Ciclovía closes many streets to cars on Sundays and holidays so people can ride.

media.credit: Sam Hidayat · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sam Hidayat

questions.description: The bravest day of childhood, scraped knees included.
questions.question: You're learning to ride a bike with training wheels, and today they come off. How many wheels does your bike have left?
hints: There were two training wheels.
Now you have to keep your balance all by yourself.
One in front and one in back.
questions.fun_fact: Many kids today first learn on a balance bike with no pedals and never use training wheels at all.

media.credit: Dawn Endico from Menlo Park, California · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dawn Endico from Menlo Park, California

questions.description: The race's appetizer, served while everyone's legs are still fresh.
questions.question: Look at the photo: this is how the prologue that opens many cycling tours is raced. What kind of race is a prologue?
hints: It's short, just a few kilometers.
It's usually held the day before the first road stage.
Whoever covers the course in the least time wins, racing against the clock.
questions.fun_fact: A prologue is usually shorter than 10 km (6 miles), but it decides who wears the first leader's jersey.

media.credit: Granada · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Granada

questions.description: If a bike wore shoes, these would be them.
questions.question: There are two of us, one for each foot. Push us down and the bike moves forward. What are we?
hints: We're down low, close to the ground.
We spin around when you ride a bike.
Your shoes rest on us while you ride.
questions.fun_fact: The first bicycles had no pedals: riders pushed themselves along with their feet on the ground.

media.credit: MacAllenBrothers · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MacAllenBrothers

questions.description: The year half of Colombia got up early to cry happy tears in front of the TV.
questions.question: In what year did Egan Bernal win the Tour de France?
hints: It was in the late 2010s.
Egan was only 22 years old.
The pandemic arrived the following year.
questions.fun_fact: Egan Bernal was the youngest Tour de France winner in more than 100 years.

media.credit: Yann Forget · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yann Forget

questions.description: Pasta, mountains and a whole lot of days on the pedals.
questions.question: Nairo Quintana and Egan Bernal both won the Giro d'Italia. Roughly how many stages does that race have?
hints: It is one of cycling's three Grand Tours, along with the Tour de France and the Vuelta a España.
It has a couple of rest days.
It lasts three weeks of seven days, nearly all with a stage.
questions.fun_fact: The trophy for the Giro winner is called the “Trofeo Senza Fine,” which means “endless,” and it is shaped like a spiral.

media.credit: Pimlico27 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pimlico27

questions.description: Sunday at the ciclovía is pure joy… until something breaks.
questions.question: It's made of metal, it needs grease, and if it slips off in the middle of the ciclovía, you have to put it back by hand. What part of the bike is it?
hints: It makes the wheels turn when you pedal.
It's made of lots of links.
It connects the pedals to the back wheel.
questions.fun_fact: The bicycle chain became common around 1885 and made it possible for both wheels to be the same size.

media.credit: Timothy J Carroll · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Timothy J Carroll

questions.description: Jumps, curves and a medal that wasn't the only Colombian one that night.
questions.question: At which Olympic Games did Carlos Oquendo win the bronze medal in BMX?
hints: It was in Europe.
That same day, Mariana Pajón won her first gold.
The city of Big Ben.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Oquendo was born in Medellín, and his bronze was the first Olympic medal won by a Colombian man in BMX.

media.credit: Fabrizio Tarizzo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fabrizio Tarizzo

questions.description: A woman from Antioquia who went around and around until she opened the way.
questions.question: I'm from Antioquia, I race on the track, and at Athens 2004 I won bronze in the points race: Colombian cycling's first Olympic medal. Who am I?
hints: I'm not a BMX rider.
I won in Greece, eight years before Mariana Pajón's first gold.
My last name is also the Spanish word for the street where cars drive.
questions.fun_fact: The points race is held in a velodrome, and riders score points in sprints every few laps.

media.credit: Rundvald · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rundvald

questions.description: The soda that's always the home team at a corrientazo lunch.
questions.question: It's a kola-flavored Postobón soda, and its slogan is “La nuestra”. Which one is it?
hints: It's golden, almost orange.
It often comes with lunch in Colombian restaurants.
Its name is the Spanish word for a woman born in Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: Postobón, the company that makes it, was founded in Medellín in 1904.

media.credit: Gerda Arendt · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerda Arendt

questions.description: The spice that makes grandma's kitchen smell like December.
questions.question: Look at the photo: these sticks go into aguapanela and arroz con leche. What part of the plant do they come from?
hints: Centuries ago it was so valuable that Europeans sailed all the way to Asia to get it.
It is cut in thin strips that curl up by themselves as they dry in the sun.
It's like the “skin” of the trunk.
questions.fun_fact: The most prized cinnamon, called Ceylon cinnamon, comes from Sri Lanka.

media.credit: Luc Viatour · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luc Viatour

questions.description: A December guest who never gets to see January 1.
questions.question: In many Colombian towns, it sits by the front door in December and is burned at midnight on the 31st. What is “el año viejo”?
hints: It is put together from the family's old clothes.
It is stuffed with sawdust, paper or rags.
It has a shirt, pants and even a face, like a person.
questions.fun_fact: Another Colombian New Year's Eve agüero (superstition) is walking around the block with a suitcase so you'll travel in the new year.

media.credit: Sgt. David Beckstrom · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sgt. David Beckstrom

questions.description: A little something between lunch and dinner, so your stomach doesn't complain.
questions.question: You're invited to “tomar onces” at 4 p.m., with hot chocolate, cheese and almojábanas. Which region of Colombia is this custom most typical of?
hints: It's a custom from the cold highlands.
There, people drink hot chocolate even in the afternoon.
It's the mountain region where the country's capital is.
questions.fun_fact: In Chile people also “toman onces”, and there it's almost a full afternoon meal.

media.credit: Peter Angritt · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Peter Angritt

questions.description: A little wooden stick with more style than many musical instruments.
questions.question: The Colombian molinillo is made of wood, has been used since colonial times and is spun by rubbing it between your palms. What is it for?
hints: It's used in a hot drink while it's still on the stove.
A Bogotá breakfast (desayuno santafereño) isn't complete without it.
Thanks to it, the drink turns out nice and foamy.
questions.fun_fact: The molinillo is used in Mexico too, and a children's song there goes “bate, bate, chocolate” (“whisk, whisk, chocolate”).

media.credit: Reginarodes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Reginarodes

questions.description: A dish that takes putting cheese on everything very seriously.
questions.question: A dessert from Colombian ice cream shops has cream, grated cheese and ice cream on top. What goes underneath, in small pieces?
hints: It's a fresh and very colorful dessert.
It all grows on trees and plants.
Mango, papaya, banana and strawberry, all cut up.
questions.fun_fact: Putting grated cheese on fruit salad is normal in Colombia, and it surprises many foreign visitors.

media.credit: Alex Robert alexrobert · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alex Robert alexrobert

questions.description: Here you can find anything, from a lulo to a good haggle over prices.
questions.question: It's nicknamed “La Minorista”, its official name is Plaza José María Villa, and it's one of Colombia's biggest markets. Which city is it in?
hints: It sits in a valley surrounded by mountains.
Its metro was the first in Colombia.
It's the city of the Feria de las Flores.
questions.fun_fact: José María Villa was the engineer who built the Puente de Occidente over the Cauca River in Santa Fe de Antioquia.

media.credit: Free Walking Tours Medellin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Free Walking Tours Medellin

questions.description: Small, tasty and the perfect snack for a day at the beach.
questions.question: On the Caribbean coast they sell ciruela costeña: small, red or yellow, and many people eat it with salt. What's in the middle?
hints: You eat it in bites, without peeling or cutting it.
You have to eat around it.
It's hard, and you don't eat it.
questions.fun_fact: The ciruela costeña is a relative of the mango and the cashew.

media.credit: Adventourscolombia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adventourscolombia

questions.description: The official snack for when school lets out.
questions.question: You're on the street and buy chopped mango biche (green mango) in a cup. What do people in Colombia usually put on it?
hints: Both are things you'll find in every kitchen.
One is white and comes in tiny grains.
The other is green and sour, and you squeeze it.
questions.fun_fact: Some people also sprinkle pepper or chili powder on their mango biche.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: The star of sancocho has a greener origin than you might think.
questions.question: Look at the photo: these are green plantains. What kind of plant do they grow on?
wrong_answers: A tree with a wooden trunk
hints: It can be taller than a person.
Its “trunk” is made of leaves rolled tightly around each other.
Its leaves are used to wrap tamales.
questions.fun_fact: A plantain plant isn't a tree: it's a giant herb, and each plant produces just one bunch.

media.credit: Henry Doe henrydoe · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Henry Doe henrydoe

questions.description: A question for people who eat everything without looking.
questions.question: Which of these fruits do you NOT need to peel before eating it?
hints: Its skin is thin, green or yellow.
Inside it's pink or white, with lots of tiny seeds.
It's used to make bocadillo veleño.
questions.fun_fact: Guava skin is edible and packed with vitamin C.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: Two actors, one shaman, and a whole lot of jungle years between them.
questions.question: In “Embrace of the Serpent”, Nilbio Torres plays the shaman Karamakate as a young man. Who plays him as an old man?
hints: He wasn't a professional actor: he was an Indigenous man from the Colombian Amazon.
He was one of the last speakers of the language of his people, the Ocaina.
He shares a last name with “the Liberator” Simón.
questions.fun_fact: Ciro Guerra's “Embrace of the Serpent” was the first Colombian film nominated for the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

media.credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC

questions.description: A blacksmith who, instead of horseshoes, forged a date on the calendar.
questions.question: Pedro Romero, a Cuban-born blacksmith, armed the artisans of his neighborhood. Under his pressure, in 1811 his city declared full independence from Spain. Which city?
hints: It is on the Caribbean coast.
Romero's artisans, armed as lancers, surrounded the government junta to demand independence.
It celebrates its independence every November 11, with festivities and a beauty pageant.
questions.fun_fact: November 11, this city's independence day, is a national holiday in Colombia, though it moves to the Monday.

media.credit: Kleseus · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kleseus

questions.description: Some people get gloomy in exile; others write the future of a continent.
questions.question: In 1815, in exile on the island in this photo, Simón Bolívar wrote a famous letter imagining the future of the Americas. Which island is it?
hints: It is in the Caribbean Sea, south of Cuba.
Its capital is Kingston.
It is the land of Usain Bolt and reggae.
questions.fun_fact: The letter was addressed to Henry Cullen, an English merchant living on the island.

media.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC

questions.description: Three cities posing in the family photo, and one that snuck in from another family.
questions.question: Which of these cities is NOT in the department of Bolívar?
hints: The odd one out is the capital of another department.
It lies near where the Magdalena River meets the sea.
It's the city of Colombia's most famous carnival.
questions.fun_fact: The historic center of Mompox was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.

media.credit: Burkhard Mücke · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Burkhard Mücke

questions.description: Long before group chats, the cities of the Valle were already starting their own group.
questions.question: In February 1811 the “Ciudades Confederadas del Valle” were born: Cali, Buga, Cartago, Toro, Anserma and Caloto. What were they?
questions.answer: A patriot alliance against the government in Popayán
wrong_answers: A pact of cities loyal to the King of Spain
A yearly fair for cattle and sugarcane
The cities founded by Sebastián de Belalcázar
hints: They came together after Cali set up its own governing junta in 1810.
Popayán was ruled by Miguel Tacón, who was loyal to the king.
They joined forces to defend themselves and avoid being ruled by royalists.
questions.fun_fact: With help from troops sent from Santafé, the confederated cities defeated Tacón at the Battle of Bajo Palacé in March 1811.

media.credit: Edgar.ivan.naranjo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Edgar.ivan.naranjo

questions.description: A fight between neighbors where one of them was born in the other's house.
questions.question: In the war between Gran Colombia and Peru (1828–1829), which of these men was NOT on Gran Colombia's side?
hints: The odd one out led the opposing army.
He was the president of Peru.
Oddly enough, he was born in Cuenca, in today's Ecuador.
questions.fun_fact: The deciding battle was Tarqui, on February 27, 1829, won by Sucre.

media.credit: Cayambe at lb.wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cayambe at lb.wikipedia

questions.description: Midnight on December 31: the only time it's normal to see your neighbor jogging with luggage.
questions.question: At New Year's in Colombia, many people walk around the block with a suitcase. What is this ritual supposed to bring?
questions.answer: Lots of travel in the new year
wrong_answers: A move to a new house
hints: It is done right at midnight on December 31.
The suitcase is the main clue.
It's a wish for airports, beaches and trips.
questions.fun_fact: Some people pack the suitcase full to make the ritual work better, and some even put their passport inside.

media.credit: Andreas Weith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andreas Weith

questions.description: Walking around uncomfortable all night pays off, or so they say.
questions.question: In Colombia, many people put a banknote inside their shoe to welcome the New Year. What is this superstition for?
hints: It has nothing to do with your feet.
What matters is what's hidden.
It's a superstition so your pockets are never empty.
questions.fun_fact: Other Colombian New Year's superstitions include eating twelve grapes, one for each chime of the clock, and carrying lentils in your pocket.

media.credit: Andy Li · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andy Li

questions.description: In the La Guajira desert, people keep the calendar by looking at the night sky.
questions.question: For the Wayuu, it is a figure in the sky that shows up at night, and its name is also used to count months. What is it called?
hints: It shines at night, but it has no light of its own.
It changes shape over the course of the month.
It is the Moon in the Wayuunaiki language.
questions.fun_fact: In Wayuu mythology, Juyá is the rain, Pulowi is his wife, and Ka'i is the Sun.

media.credit: ESO/B.Tafreshi (twanight.org) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author:
ESO/B.Tafreshi (twanight.org) 


.

questions.description: The smallest, shiniest bodyguard a baby can have.
questions.question: Many Colombian babies wear a little bracelet with an azabache to protect them from the evil eye. What is an azabache?
hints: It's hard and shines when polished.
It forms from fossilized wood, like coal.
Its English name, jet, is also the name of a very dark color.
questions.fun_fact: The belief goes that if the azabache cracks or breaks, it took the evil eye in the baby's place.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: The saddest long-distance relationship in Colombian literature.
questions.question: In the novel “María,” Efraín's father sends him far from the hacienda and from María to study medicine. Which city does he go to?
hints: He has to cross the Atlantic Ocean.
It is a European city where people don't speak Spanish.
It is the capital of England.
questions.fun_fact: El Paraíso, the hacienda where the novel takes place, really exists in Valle del Cauca and is now a museum.

media.credit: Diego Carrejo Murillo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Carrejo Murillo

questions.description: Before it reached your cup, your tinto lived in a little red berry hanging from a bush.
questions.question: You're on a coffee farm and open a ripe coffee cherry. How many beans are almost always inside?
hints: Very few: you can count them on one hand.
Each bean has a flat side facing its neighbor inside the cherry.
It's a pair.

You should think before you speak

To treat someone to a coffee

A puff pastry cake with cream

It came out a few years after “El capo”.
It premiered the same year some people said the world was going to end.

hints: She is a young Colombian actress.
This was her first major leading role.
She shares a surname with a former president of Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: “Siempre bruja” is based on the novel “Yo, bruja” by Colombian writer Isidora Chacón.

questions.description: A trip with heat, goats, dunes and an accordion playing in the background.
questions.question: You’re on a trip through La Guajira, vallenato country. Which of these cities will you NOT find there?

questions.question: In which century did Francisco de Paula Santander, the “Man of the Laws,” govern?

He governed when the country had just won independence from Spain.

questions.fun_fact: The department of Santander is named after him, though he was born in Villa del Rosario, which is now in Norte de Santander.

People called him “the Great General.”
A town in Cundinamarca, next to Bogotá, bears his surname.
questions.fun_fact: A decree by Mosquera in November 1861 adopted the yellow, blue and red flag with horizontal stripes, almost the same as today's.

hints: The country was split into nine sovereign states.
Its great promoter was General Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera.
It copies the official name of the country whose capital is Washington.
questions.fun_fact: The country kept that name for 23 years, until the Constitution of 1886 changed it to Republic of Colombia.

questions.question: In the 19th century, on the steep Quindío trail, the silleteros carried a chair strapped to their backs. What did they carry in that chair?
hints: It was a muddy track where mules could barely get through.
Sometimes the load complained about the trip.
Today, for that same service, you would pay a fare.
questions.fun_fact: The flowers came much later: since 1957, silleteros have paraded with their silletas at Medellín's Feria de las Flores.

questions.question: Your mesada (allowance) is 3,000 pesos a week and you spend none of it. How much money do you save in 4 weeks?
hints: It's a simple multiplication.

It's what a 10,000 bill and a 2,000 bill add up to.

hints: Look for the one with no jungle around it.
The other three are in the Amazonas department, in the south of the country.
It's an island in the Caribbean Sea.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon is home to the pink river dolphin, which swims in rivers, not in the sea.

hints: It has nothing to do with real windows.

It's the same fiber your T-shirts are made of.

It started about ten years ago and closed a few years later.

It was played in South America.

Cabo de la Vela is there.

questions.question: You're watching TV as the presidential sash is placed on the new president in Bogotá. What date is it?
hints: It's a national holiday.
The day commemorates a battle.
It was the Battle of Boyacá, in 1819.
questions.fun_fact: The presidential sash has the colors of the flag and Colombia's coat of arms embroidered on it.

media.author: Javierleiva

questions.description: The time of year when the flag goes out for a stroll through every window.
questions.question: They come in July and August, flags hang from houses and there are independence parades. What are these celebrations called?
hints: Schools hold flag-raising ceremonies for these dates.
One is on July 20 and the other on August 7.
They celebrate the Grito de Independencia and the Battle of Boyacá: the birth of the nation.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, July 20 and August 7 are public holidays that are never moved to a Monday.

media.author: National Police of Colombia

hints: Brazil took the lead, and Colombia came back to win.
Both goals came late in the match.
Two crosses came in from the wing, and he jumped higher than the Brazilian defenders.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won 2-1, and Luis Díaz scored both goals in just four minutes after Brazil had taken the lead.

media.credit: Daveborge · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daveborge

questions.description: A bunch of teenage girls who went further than plenty of grown-ups.
questions.question: In what year did Colombia play its first final of a FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup, in India, against Spain?
hints: It was after the pandemic.
Linda Caicedo was already playing for the senior national team that year.
It was the year Argentina won the World Cup in Qatar.
questions.fun_fact: Spain won that final 1–0 and Colombia finished runner-up, with Linda Caicedo just 17 years old.

media.author: Debnathsonu1996

questions.description: A wall that came from the Pacific coast and learned to defend in Belgium.
questions.question: I was born in Quibdó in 1999, came up through Atlético Nacional and played several years for Genk in Belgium. I'm a center back for Colombia. Who am I?
hints: I'm the youngest of the four.
After Belgium I played for Galatasaray in Turkey.
My last name is the Spanish word for a steep slope.
questions.fun_fact: Quibdó, the capital of Chocó, is one of the rainiest cities in the world.

media.author: Mussi Katz from Israel

questions.description: An acronym that sounds like a tongue twister and looked after half the country.
questions.question: From 1968 I managed Colombia's natural resources and created many national parks; in 1993 the Ministry of the Environment replaced me. What was my name?
hints: I was a government institute.
My name was an acronym that started with “In”.
My acronym included “recursos naturales renovables” (renewable natural resources).
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park, Cueva de los Guácharos, was created in 1960, before this institute even existed.

media.credit: Alaincho67 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alaincho67

questions.description: A star that doesn't shine in the sky but flows through the jungle.
questions.question: A Ramsar wetland in Guainía is named after the Inírida, Guaviare and Atabapo rivers, which meet there. Which great river do its waters flow into?
hints: It's one of the longest rivers in South America.
Alexander von Humboldt traveled along it and studied it in 1800.
It gives its name to one of Colombia's great natural regions, the Llanos.
questions.fun_fact: Nearby rise the Mavecure hills, giant rocks that are among the oldest on the planet.

media.credit: Lamoraleja · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lamoraleja

questions.description: Nature is free, but taking care of it costs a bit of plata.
questions.question: In Colombia's national parks, like Tayrona, who pays the highest entrance fee?
hints: Not everyone pays the same.
It depends on where the visitor comes from.
They come from other countries.
questions.fun_fact: The money from entrance fees helps pay for trails, park rangers and conservation programs.

media.credit: Adventourscolombia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adventourscolombia

questions.description: A flower that flat-out refuses to wilt.
questions.question: It's a red flower that lasts a very long time without wilting, grows on sandy savannas and is named after a jungle capital. Which department is it from?
hints: It's a department in eastern Colombia, on the border.
It borders Venezuela and Brazil.
Its capital is Inírida.
questions.fun_fact: It's called the “eternal flower” because even after it's cut, it keeps its color for a long time.

media.credit: Gicaman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gicaman

questions.description: A trophy you don't win by jumping for joy… although in this case, it helped quite a bit.
questions.question: In 2018, Caterine Ibargüen became the first Colombian to receive a major international award. Which one?
hints: In 2018 she won almost every competition she entered.
Usain Bolt received it several times.
It goes to whoever had the best track and field season on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: That same year, the men's award went to Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge, who had just broken the marathon world record.

media.credit: elfgoh. · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: elfgoh.

questions.description: Some people lift weights, and some people lift a whole country.
questions.question: Weightlifter María Isabel Urrutia is one of the great stars of Colombian sport. Which department is she from?
hints: It's a department with a coast on the Pacific Ocean.
She was born in Candelaria, a town very close to the department's capital.
Its capital is the city of salsa, the “Sucursal del Cielo”.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, María Isabel Urrutia became Colombia's Minister of Sport.

media.credit: Cobragym1 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cobragym1

questions.description: A man who can lift more than a whole stadium's spirits.
questions.question: I'm a Colombian weightlifter. At Rio 2016 I got bronze after a rival was disqualified, and at Tokyo 2020 I won silver. Who am I?
hints: I compete in one of the lightest weight classes.
In Tokyo I competed in the 67 kg class.
My last name is also the name of a town in Cundinamarca.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won no gold at Tokyo 2020: it came home with four silvers and one bronze.

media.author: Santeri Viinamäki

questions.description: In January, Melbourne burns, and not just from the sun: the rackets are on fire too.
questions.question: Which Colombian tennis player won the 2017 Australian Open mixed doubles with American Abigail Spears?
hints: He is a doubles specialist.
He was born in Cali in 1986.
He shares his first names with the navigator Elcano.
questions.fun_fact: That mixed doubles title in Melbourne was the first Grand Slam of his career.

media.author: Hameltion

questions.description: A game where butter is your worst enemy.
questions.question: At town festivals, people put up a very tall pole covered in grease, with prizes at the top, and try to climb it. What is it called?
hints: Almost everyone slips before reaching the top.
Contestants stand on each other's shoulders to make it.
In Spanish, “sebo” is another word for grease.
questions.fun_fact: Games like the palo encebado exist in many countries, from the Philippines to Italy.

media.author: apium from Northern Virginia, U.S.A.

questions.question: Its creator was a painter born in Medellín, and in this style everything looks huge and round: people, fruit and even horses. What is it called?
hints: Its sculptures stand in squares of cities all over the world.
Its creator gave many sculptures to a square in downtown Medellín.
The painter's first name was Fernando.
questions.fun_fact: Botero said he didn't paint fat people: he painted volume, because he loved how big shapes fill a canvas.

media.credit: Jose Diez · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jose Diez

questions.description: A pop idol, a can of spray paint and a national scandal: the perfect recipe for the evening news.
questions.question: In what year did Justin Bieber spray-paint graffiti on a wall on Bogotá's Calle 26 during a concert tour?
hints: It was during a world tour that took him through several Latin American countries.
It happened in the 2010s.
It was the same year Pope Francis was elected.
questions.fun_fact: It caused an uproar because Bieber painted with a police escort, while many Bogotá graffiti artists complained that police chased them for doing the same.

media.author: Paul from Hacketts Cove, Canada

questions.description: A work of art that literally hit the floor.
questions.question: I'm an artist from Bogotá. In 2007 I opened a 167 m (548 ft) crack in the floor of London's Tate Modern and called it “Shibboleth.” Who am I?
hints: My works deal with memory and the victims of violence.
In 2018 I made a floor from melted-down FARC weapons, called “Fragmentos.”
My first name starts with D.
questions.fun_fact: The crack of “Shibboleth” was filled in after the exhibition ended, but the scar is still visible in the Tate's floor.

media.credit: Daniel X. O'Neil · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel X. O'Neil

questions.question: During Holy Week in Popayán, what are the men called who carry floats like the one in this photo on their shoulders?
hints: Popayán's processions have gone out at night since colonial times and are UNESCO heritage.
They walk under the float's poles, with a cushion on the shoulder.
Their name comes from the Spanish verb “cargar”, meaning “to carry”.
questions.fun_fact: In Popayán, being a carguero often passes from father to son, and some families carry the same float for generations.

media.author: DavidSMSilva

questions.description: A head of hair that deserves its own sticker album.
questions.question: El Pibe Valderrama played in three World Cups in a row for Colombia's national team. In which decade were they?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
One of those World Cups was played in the United States.
They were Italy, the United States and France, one every four years.
questions.fun_fact: In 1987, El Pibe became the first Colombian named South American Footballer of the Year.

media.credit: Krzysztof Popławski · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Krzysztof Popławski

questions.description: A man who lived in a castle without being a king or a fairy-tale character.
questions.question: I was a philanthropist from Antioquia, lived in a Medellín castle that is now a museum, and gave Itagüí its first library. Who am I?
hints: My family was behind some of Antioquia's big textile companies.
I bought the castle in the 1940s and filled it with European art and furniture.
The library in Itagüí carries my full name.
questions.fun_fact: Museo El Castillo, in El Poblado, copies the medieval castles of France and has gardens open to the public.

media.credit: Zack Knowles · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zack Knowles

At the tip of each “hair” there's a tiny bit of pollen.
They are the male part of the flower.
questions.fun_fact: The carbonero's petals are so tiny and greenish that hardly anyone notices them.

media.author: sarahemcc

questions.description: A flower so elegant it has more cousins than a paisa family in December.
questions.question: Colombia is one of the countries with the most orchid species in the world. About how many does it have?
hints: Colombia is one of the most biodiverse countries on the planet.
A single cloud forest reserve can have hundreds of orchid species.
It's thousands, but not tens of thousands.
questions.fun_fact: More than 1,500 of Colombia's orchids grow in no other country.

questions.question: I’m a woman from Colombia’s Pacific coast: in the arrullos I sing the lead and the others answer me in chorus, to the cununo drum. What am I?
hints: You find me at wakes and saints’ festivals in Guapi, Timbiquí or Tumaco.
The women who answer me in the chorus are called “respondedoras.”
My name comes from the Spanish verb for what I do with my throat.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, UNESCO declared the marimba music and traditional chants of Colombia’s South Pacific region an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

media.author: Juandareina

She also doesn't want them eating the mice's bigger cousins for dinner.
They love cheese and are scared of cats.
questions.fun_fact: «Candonga» is an old word for someone sweet-talking and crafty, perfect for a flirty cat.

It was the same year as Shakira's session with Bizarrap.
questions.fun_fact: “TQG” stands for “Te Quedó Grande.”

media.author: PinkBeachPlanet

Time heals it… and so does despecho music.
It happens when your boyfriend or girlfriend leaves you.

It's in the second half of the year.
It's the month for flying kites in Colombia.

He was born the same year as the great New York stock market crash.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Villamil was an orthopedic surgeon who wrote songs in his spare time; many of them sing about the landscapes of Huila.

It moves along rivers with a paddle.
questions.fun_fact: Many towns in Chocó have no roads: the rivers are the highways, and almost everything travels by canoe.

It sounds almost like a baby crying.
questions.fun_fact: In Cuba and the Canary Islands a “guagua” is a bus, so if you ask for one in Havana, nobody will hand you a baby.

There's a chicken one, a fish one and even a “trifásico” one.
questions.fun_fact: Sancocho “trifásico” gets its name because it has three meats: beef, pork and chicken.

media.author: Rodolfo pimentel

Its name starts with “Risa”.
questions.fun_fact: The Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, which includes part of Risaralda, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.

questions.description: A road trip with a sea breeze that someone crashed wearing rubber boots.

questions.fun_fact: Florencia, the capital of Caquetá, is known as “the golden gateway to the Colombian Amazon.”

media.author: Vinicius

Its name has only two syllables and ends in “ú.”

questions.fun_fact: The Cerros de Mavecure are rocks more than a billion years old that rise like towers out of the jungle.

It splits in two, and one branch runs into Venezuela.
It's on the side where the sun rises over Colombia.

questions.answer: A religious cloth worn around the neck

A rosary of beads used for praying
A small pouch for keeping tobacco

Many drivers also hang one in the car.
It almost always carries the image of the Virgen del Carmen.

You use just one, not two as in knitting.
Its curved tip catches the yarn.

hints: Touch it with your fingertips.

It's made of very fine little hairs.
questions.fun_fact: The peach comes from China, even though its scientific name, Prunus persica, points to Persia.

hints: It's for drinking, not chewing.

It's served in a glass, sometimes with ice.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia you can buy frozen pulp of loads of fruits, from mora and lulo to guanábana and corozo.

hints: He is the central figure of the prayer.
In Christian tradition, he is the one who will judge everyone at the end of time.
He was born in Bethlehem.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombian drivers hang holy cards or rosaries from the rearview mirror to protect them on the road.

I share my last name with a 20th-century Colombian president.
questions.fun_fact: The 1992 Miss Universe pageant, where Paola Turbay came second, was held in Bangkok, Thailand.

hints: I didn’t write the anthem’s words: a president took care of that.
I stayed in Bogotá and taught music for many years.
My name sounds very Italian and starts with O.
questions.fun_fact: Síndici stayed in Colombia for the rest of his life and died in Bogotá in 1904.

hints: In this way, it looks like its big cousin, the condor.
It helps the bird stay clean when it eats dead animals.
If you look closely, it seems to be bald.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the gallinazo is also called “chulo” or “golero,” depending on the region.

hints: The name is said to come from Quechua, the language of the Incas.
It has to do with an animal of the Andes.
That animal is now Colombia's national bird.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá is the capital of Cundinamarca, although as a Capital District it is run separately from the department.

hints: It is not created by the government, but by private individuals.
Its name refers to ordinary people, not the government.
Its name contains the word “civil”.

hints: They come from very far away, sometimes from North America.
They travel through the air.
They have feathers and move to a different place depending on the time of year.
questions.fun_fact: The tingua bogotana (Bogotá rail) is a bird that lives only in the wetlands of the Bogotá high plateau and the area around it.

They were won by a weightlifter, a female BMX rider and a female triple jumper.
questions.fun_fact: In total, Colombia brought home 8 medals from Rio: 3 gold, 2 silver and 3 bronze.

The name sounds like the whole planet is playing, not just one continent.

The ball is hit against the front wall of an enclosed court.
questions.fun_fact: Squash was born in England, at Harrow School, around 1830.

hints: I'm made of metal.
Inside me there's a little ball that rattles when you shake me.
Press the little button on top and the paint comes out as a fine mist.
questions.fun_fact: Spray paint cans have a little ball inside that mixes the paint when you shake them: that's why they go “clack, clack”.

questions.question: The yipao is a Willys jeep loaded to the roof with coffee, plantains or a family’s furniture, and it has its own parade. In which department did that parade begin?
hints: It’s one of Colombia’s smallest departments.
The Cocora Valley, with its wax palms, is there.
Its capital is Armenia.
questions.fun_fact: In the Coffee Axis, “un yipao” is also a unit of measure: whatever fits in a fully loaded Willys.

questions.question: In many versions of the tale, a doll is placed on Tío Conejo’s path to catch him. What is it made of?
hints: The rabbit hits the doll because it doesn’t answer his greeting.
With every blow he gets more stuck: his paws won’t come loose.
It’s the sticky black stuff once used to seal wooden ships.
questions.fun_fact: The same tale exists in the southern United States, where the doll is called the “Tar-Baby” and the one who falls for the trap is Br’er Rabbit.

hints: It was long before Columbus reached the Americas.
Around the same time, the first Gothic cathedrals were going up.
We’re talking about the 11th to 13th centuries, in southern France.
questions.fun_fact: The first troubadours didn’t sing in French but in Occitan, a language of southern France.

questions.description: A word so soft it sounds like a cat purring.

questions.answer: To put a baby to sleep
hints: It’s sung at night.
It goes with gentle rocking in someone’s arms.
It’s the word that fills lullabies.
questions.fun_fact: In other countries the same lullaby is sung with “arrorró” instead of “arrurrú”.

hints: As a teenager, I took part in a talent show on Colombian TV.
In 2023 I released a worldwide hit with Shakira.
My album “Mañana Será Bonito” reached number 1 in the United States.
questions.fun_fact: Provenza is an area of bars and restaurants in the El Poblado neighborhood of Medellín, and it became even more famous after the song.

hints: It's a single word that refers to a place, not a rhythm.
On the Caribbean coast, people use it to talk about Valledupar and the area around it.
In Spanish, it's what Argentina and Ecuador call their main divisions.
questions.fun_fact: With “Clásicos de la Provincia,” Carlos Vives recorded old vallenatos with a rock and pop sound and took them around the world.

It became one of his catchiest songs of those years.
What makes him rich is being with the person he loves.

hints: Its roots go back much farther than Europe.

Their communities are organized in kumpañy.

questions.description: A rhythm with dual citizenship, or at least a double name.

questions.question: I'm a region of flat savannas, my rivers flow to the Orinoco, and my men wear a liqui liqui and a hat to parties. Which region am I?
hints: I share these savannas with Venezuela.
Joropo is danced here with harp, cuatro and maracas.
Villavicencio is my gateway.
questions.fun_fact: The liqui liqui is typical of the plains of Colombia and Venezuela, and in Venezuela it's considered the national men's outfit.

media.author: Wladimir Labeikovsky

questions.description: The accessory that turns any head into an arriero's head.
questions.question: It's white with a black band, woven from iraca palm in a town in Caldas and worn by paisa arrieros. What is it called?
hints: Its town is in northern Caldas, near Antioquia.
That town holds the Festival Nacional del Pasillo.
Its name comes from the municipality of Aguadas.
questions.fun_fact: A good iraca hat is woven by hand, strand by strand, and can take several days to finish.

media.credit: Juan Gómez · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Gómez

questions.description: A headdress so colorful it would make a parrot cry with envy.
questions.question: Among Indigenous peoples of the Colombian Amazon, the macaw-feather crown is worn at ceremonies and dances. What does it show about the wearer?
questions.answer: That they are an important person
wrong_answers: That it is their birthday today
That rain will come very soon
That they are leaving on a trip
hints: Not just anyone can put it on.
It is often worn by the shaman or the community's leaders.
It means something similar to a king's crown.
questions.fun_fact: Macaws, whose feathers adorn these crowns, can live for more than 50 years.

media.author: Garst, Warren, 1922-2016, photographer

questions.description: Out of the lake come fish, ducks and… this craft.
questions.question: At Laguna de Fúquene, people cut reeds, dry them in the sun and weave them into esteras. What is an estera?
questions.answer: A flat weave to spread on the floor
wrong_answers: A basket with a handle for the market
A hat with a wide brim
A bag to carry on the shoulder
hints: Families around the lake have woven them for generations.
It used to be common in farmhouses, and today it's sold as a craft at markets.
When it's not in use, you roll it up.
questions.fun_fact: The reeds and cattails of Fúquene are also woven into baskets, placemats and even furniture.

media.credit: Adgrant96 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adgrant96

questions.description: A parade with no floats, no music, and nobody who wants to go and watch it.
questions.question: In the villages they say that at midnight a silent line of figures with candles passes down the street, praying. Who are they?
hints: They are no longer of this world.
They ask people to pray for them.
In Colombia they're called the ánimas del purgatorio.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that if someone accepts a candle from the procession, by the next morning it has turned into a bone.

media.credit: Julia Folsom · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Julia Folsom

questions.description: The cheapest security system in the world: no alarm, no cameras, just one of Grandma's tricks.
questions.question: Grandmas say that to keep a witch out of the house, you leave a metal object opened into a cross behind the door. Which one?
hints: Almost every home has them in a drawer somewhere.
Two metal parts joined in the middle.
They have two holes for your fingers.
questions.fun_fact: Some people also put them in a cross under the pillow to sleep without nightmares.

media.credit: Kızıl · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kızıl

questions.description: A dance where Death joins the party and keeps losing.
questions.question: At the Barranquilla Carnival, the Garabato dancers fight against Death. What is the garabato they carry in their hand?
hints: The dancers hold it up high and wave it as they dance.
It is decorated with flowers and colorful ribbons.
Its tip is bent, like a question mark.
questions.fun_fact: In the Garabato dance, Life beats Death, so the dance ends in a big party.

media.credit: Eddy Milfort · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eddy Milfort

questions.description: A general who switched sides faster than a fan whose team is losing.
questions.question: In 1812, during the Patria Boba, Antonio Baraya, the hero of Palacé, switched sides. Whom did he turn against?
hints: He was the centralist leader of Cundinamarca.
He translated and printed the Declaration of the Rights of Man.
Later, in 1814, he was captured in Pasto.
questions.fun_fact: In 1811 Baraya won the Battle of Bajo Palacé, one of the first patriot victories in New Granada.

media.credit: JuanGris (Lucía Estévez) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JuanGris (Lucía Estévez)

questions.description: While others fought with sabers, this gentleman fought with letters and seals.
questions.question: I was born in Caracas, served as foreign minister of Gran Colombia, was a delegate to the 1826 Congress of Panama and, in old age, president of Venezuela. Who am I?
hints: My job was dealing with other countries, not commanding troops.
I signed treaties with Mexico, Peru and Central America.
My first name is the same as the first pope’s.
questions.fun_fact: The 1826 Congress of Panama, promoted by Bolívar, was one of the first attempts to unite the countries of the Americas.

media.credit: Moore, J. Hampton (Joseph Hampton), 1864-1950 · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Moore, J. Hampton (Joseph Hampton), 1864-1950

questions.description: The most dangerous house in Santafé had no cannons, just needles and thread.
questions.question: In which patriot woman's house in Santafé did Policarpa Salavarrieta live while plotters against the Reconquista met there?
hints: Like other patriot women, she took risks to help the cause of independence.
She was married to a Lozano.
Her last name is the same as a hero of San Mateo.
questions.fun_fact: Policarpa got into royalist homes as a seamstress and gathered information for the patriots that way.

media.credit: Racso (Oscar Fernando Gómez) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Racso (Oscar Fernando Gómez)

questions.description: Somebody had to do the paperwork while Bolívar posed for paintings.
questions.question: I was born in La Guaira, served as Bolívar's chief of staff in the 1819 Liberation Campaign and was later president of Venezuela twice. Who am I?
hints: I didn't command the vanguard or the rear guard at Boyacá.
Later I was a Venezuelan minister and diplomat.
I governed Venezuela in the 1830s and 1840s.
questions.fun_fact: Soublette died in 1870 at age 80, one of the few heroes of independence who lived to old age.

media.credit: Kamilokardona · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kamilokardona

questions.description: Antioquia didn't wait for anyone's permission to say “that's it, we're done.”
questions.question: Every August 11, Antioquia remembers when Juan del Corral declared its complete independence from Spain. What year was it?
hints: It was during the Patria Boba.
It was before Pablo Morillo arrived.
It was the same year as Bolívar's Admirable Campaign.
questions.fun_fact: Juan del Corral also pushed for a “free womb” law in Antioquia: children born to enslaved women would be born free.

media.credit: Carlos Chalarca · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Chalarca

questions.description: Bogotá has two guardians on the mountain, and one of them wears a Virgin on its head.
questions.question: Guadalupe Hill, with its big statue of the Virgin Mary, watches over Bogotá from the eastern hills. Roughly how high is its summit?
hints: Bogotá itself is already very high: about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft) above sea level.
From the top you can see the whole city, and up there it's often cold and foggy.
Its summit is over 3,000 meters, but nowhere near as high as the snowy peaks.
questions.fun_fact: The statue of the Virgin of Guadalupe on the summit is about 15 meters (49 ft) tall and can be seen from much of Bogotá.

media.credit: Tisquesusa · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tisquesusa

questions.description: A church with vertigo: it lives hanging over an abyss and never complains.
questions.question: The Las Lajas sanctuary, in Ipiales, rises over the canyon of the Guáitara River. Why was it built right there?
questions.answer: Because of an image of the Virgin in the rock
wrong_answers: Because of a gold mine at the bottom
To keep watch over the border with Ecuador
hints: Every year thousands of visitors come from Colombia and Ecuador.
According to legend, a mother and her daughter saw something on a stone in the canyon in the 18th century.
The church rests against the canyon wall, and that stone became its altar.
questions.fun_fact: The current church, in Gothic style, was finished in 1949 and is counted around the world among the most beautiful churches.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: A cave with a full set of teeth and not a dentist in sight.
questions.question: Look at the photo: spikes hanging from a cave ceiling, like in the caves of Santander. What are they made of?
hints: They don't melt in the heat.
They form from drops of water carrying dissolved minerals.
That's why they are rock-hard and don't bend.
questions.fun_fact: A stalactite can take about 100 years to grow just 1 centimeter (less than half an inch).

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: Bogotá: the only place where you leave home in sunglasses and need an umbrella three blocks later.
questions.question: In Bogotá it can rain in one neighborhood while the sun shines in another, as the hills and wind give each area its own climate. What is such a small-area climate called?
hints: It's a climate in a small size.
A valley, a neighborhood or even a garden can have one.
Its name starts with a prefix that means “very small.”
questions.fun_fact: Because of its mountains, Colombia has neighboring towns with very different climates, one cold and one hot.

media.credit: Peter Angritt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Peter Angritt

questions.description: A natural shower in Santander, except the showerhead is up in the clouds.
questions.question: The Juan Curí waterfalls, near San Gil, are among the most visited in Santander. About how tall are they?
hints: They are much taller than a two-story house.
They are taller than a 40-story building.
They are close to 200 meters.
questions.fun_fact: At Juan Curí you can go down the wall of the waterfall hanging from a rope, rappelling.

media.credit: Pedro Alejandro Ariza Rubiano · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pedro Alejandro Ariza Rubiano

questions.description: A capital-city flag that doesn’t need three stripes to show off.
questions.question: Bogotá’s flag has just two horizontal stripes of the same size. What colors are they?
hints: Its colors date back to the days of independence in Bogotá.
One of its colors is also on the flag of Colombia.
They are the colors of the sun and of fire.
questions.fun_fact: Its colors come from the yellow and red armbands that patriots wore in Bogotá on July 20, 1810.

media.author: Jos Cuevasc

questions.description: A sticker album where an intruder sneaked in.
questions.question: You're watching the 2024 Copa América in your yellow shirt. Which of these players was NOT on Colombia's national team?
hints: He doesn't wear the yellow shirt, but a striped one.
He ended up lifting that Copa with his own team.
He wears Argentina's number 10.
questions.fun_fact: Even though Colombia lost the final, James Rodríguez was named the best player of that Copa América.

questions.description: A man whose whole job is making sure nothing happens.
questions.question: I'm a goalkeeper, I played for Arsenal in England and Napoli in Italy, and I was Colombia's starter at the 2014 and 2018 World Cups. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Medellín in 1988.
I have played more games for the Selección than anyone in its history.
I share my first name with the boy who beat the giant Goliath.
questions.fun_fact: Ospina played more than 120 games for Colombia, more than any other player.

media.credit: Santeri Viinamäki · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Santeri Viinamäki

questions.question: For Colombia, the number 10 shirt has been worn by el Pibe Valderrama and James Rodríguez. What does the player with that number usually do?
questions.answer: Create plays and set up goals
wrong_answers: Guard the box as last defender
hints: He plays in the middle, close to the strikers.
People call him the “brain” or the “playmaker” of the team.
He's the one who serves the ball on a plate to the goal scorer.
questions.fun_fact: Giving the 10 to the team's star became famous with Pelé, who wore it at the 1958 World Cup.

He scored three goals at that World Cup, all headers.
He celebrates his goals by dancing.
questions.fun_fact: Yerry Mina scored three headed goals at Russia 2018: against Poland, Senegal and England.

media.author: Brateevsky

hints: Before Colombia, he coached this country's national team at the 2006 World Cup.
With this country, he won three Under-20 World Cups.
It's Messi's country.
questions.fun_fact: With Pékerman, Colombia went back to a World Cup in 2014 after 16 years away.

wrong_answers: Watch the animals without touching them
hints: Three of these things protect nature.
The thing you shouldn't do can harm the animals and the sea.
You have to take your bags and bottles back with you.
questions.fun_fact: In Tayrona, visitors must carry out of the park all the trash they bring in.

To repair it later with the pieces
To sell it to a museum later

Think about what Medellín was going through in the 1990s.
The new sculpture has the opposite of war in its name.

Its English name joins the word for the church's holy table with the word “piece”.

media.author: Dvwoud09 at English Wikipedia

The name “Kokoriko” sounds like a rooster’s crow.

media.author: Tomascastelazo

I became famous around the world at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

questions.fun_fact: Even though Colombia lost the final, James was named the best player of the 2024 Copa América.

His first name is Gonzalo.

questions.description: A castle with no princesses or dragons, but a very unfriendly face.

media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: The voice that coaxed the most coins out of a jukebox on a Sunday afternoon.

My first name recalls the mountain of the Greek gods.
questions.fun_fact: Olimpo Cárdenas spent so many years in Colombia that many Colombians thought of him as one of their own.

media.author: Garry Knight from London, England

questions.description: A trip to southern Huila isn't over without a full bag for the road.

questions.description: A character of the Colombian streets who never needed GPS.
questions.question: I work on the street with a rag in my hand. When you go to park, I wave and shout “¡siga, siga, siga!” Who am I?
hints: You find me outside shops and restaurants.
At the end, you give me a few coins.
I tell you when to stop before you crash.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “siga” is also the polite way to say “come in” when someone arrives at your home.

questions.description: A saying that comes with its own weather forecast.
questions.question: It rains on the day of the family outing and your mom says “al mal tiempo, buena cara.” Why does she say it?
questions.answer: To cheer you up even if things go wrong
wrong_answers: To get you to put on your raincoat
To tell you the outing is canceled
To scold you for getting wet
hints: It has nothing to do with clothes.
It’s about attitude.
It’s like saying: smile even if things don’t go the way you wanted.
questions.fun_fact: This saying came from Spain and is used all over Latin America, not only when it rains.

questions.description: A family inheritance nobody wants, and scientists have been chasing it for over 30 years.
questions.question: A mutation in the PSEN1 gene causes Alzheimer's before age 50 in thousands of relatives studied by Francisco Lopera. Where do they live?
hints: It's the Colombian region with the most families in the world affected by this mutation.
Neurologist Francisco Lopera worked at that region's public university.
The mutation was nicknamed after what people from Medellín are called.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists see these families as a unique chance to test treatments that could slow Alzheimer's before any symptoms appear.

questions.description: Before social media, the news in Santafé arrived on paper with the ink still fresh.
questions.question: Born in Bayamo, Cuba, he ran the Royal Library of Santafé and founded the Papel Periódico de Santafé de Bogotá. Who was he?
hints: He came to Santafé as a librarian, not as a politician or soldier.
He is considered the father of Colombian journalism.
His middle name is also a title of the Virgin Mary.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Library he ran is the forerunner of the Biblioteca Nacional de Colombia.

questions.description: A scientist who studied Colombian families and now lives in all of their wallets.
questions.question: When you pay with a new 10,000-peso bill, you see the face of the anthropologist who studied the families of Colombia's regions. Who is she?
hints: She was one of the country's first anthropologists.
She wrote “Familia y cultura en Colombia.”
She was born in El Socorro, Santander.
questions.fun_fact: Her 1968 book “Familia y cultura en Colombia” showed that the family changes enormously from one region of the country to another.

questions.description: A character who, the moment they say hello, is already telling you where they're from and why their land is the best.
questions.question: I was born in the capital of Norte de Santander, by the bridge that crosses into Venezuela, and I love pasteles de garbanzo. What am I?
hints: My city is one of the hottest in the Santanders.
Right next to my city, the congress that created Gran Colombia met in 1821.
The name of my city starts with “Cú”.
questions.fun_fact: In Villa del Rosario, right next to Cúcuta, the Constitution of Gran Colombia was written in 1821.

questions.description: Twenty Antioquians, machetes and mules: the most ambitious weekend plan in history.
questions.question: In 1848, settlers from Neira and Salamina made the “Expedición de los Veinte” to pick the site for a new city. Which city was founded there in 1849?
hints: It's part of the Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero).
Today it's the capital of a department created in 1905.
Its January fair has a famous international coffee beauty pageant.
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century, the Antioquian colonization founded dozens of towns in the mountains of west-central Colombia.

questions.description: A city that exists because someone gave away a plot of land, and not for a parking lot.
questions.question: Who donated the land on which the city of Cúcuta was founded in 1733?
hints: The donated land lay in the valley of the Pamplonita River.
She gave it so the neighbors could build a church dedicated to Saint Joseph.
That's why people say Cúcuta was founded by a woman.
questions.fun_fact: The donation was signed on June 17, 1733, the date taken as Cúcuta's founding.

questions.description: A song that made half the country sigh in front of the TV at dinnertime.
questions.question: Which Colombian telenovela has the opening song “¿Quién es ese hombre?”?
hints: It premiered in 2003 and became famous in many countries.
It tells the story of three brothers who come to a hacienda for revenge.
The Reyes brothers fall in love with the Elizondo sisters.

Her story took place a few decades after Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded Tunja in 1539.

questions.question: It's measured in points every night, and if it's too low, a telenovela can be taken off the air. What is it?
hints: It shows up in the entertainment news the next day.
Caracol and RCN fight over it every night.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Betty, la fea,” what is the name of Ecomoda's vice president of sales, Armando Mendoza's best friend?

I’m named after what you do when you say “¡quiubo!” to someone.
